About: gravitational lensing of a small source by a point mass, from resolved images to microlensing

About this simulation

On screen
Left: the sky about the lens in units of the Einstein radius θE, from −2.5 to 2.5 θE. The grey dot is the lens, the dashed circle is the Einstein ring and the dotted circle is the true position of the source on its dashed path. The pale patches are the images, lit by inverse ray shooting at the source's own surface brightness. The translucent grey disc is the 0.1 arcsec resolution of a large telescope on the same scale. Right: the total magnification A against t/tE, measured in blue light and in red light.
Controls
Lens mass M from 0.1 to 1013 M⊙ and lens distance DL from 1 kpc to 1 Gpc, both on logarithmic scales; changing them keeps the time and the traces. Closest approach u0 (η0 in the Fermi Notes, §9.3, eqs. 9.32–9.35, where u is η) from 0.10 to 1.00 θE; changing it returns t to −2 tE and clears the traces. ▶ Play runs t/tE from −2 to +2 at 0.5 per second, once.
Measured
θE and tE from the Einstein-ring and crossing-time relations with DS = 2DL and a transverse speed of 200 km/s; u, A and the image positions from the point-lens equation. The separation is θ+ − θ− in arcsec. All of these appear in the Readouts panel in the sidebar; tE and a human lifetime for scale appear from question 6 on.
Simplifications
The lens is a single point mass; a real galaxy is extended, so its images and magnifications differ from these (the point-mass model is exact for a star or a compact object). Distances add as in flat, static space (DLS = DS − DL), which is only approximate at Gpc distances, where cosmological angular-diameter distances apply. A is for a point source; the drawn source has a small finite size. Lens, source and observer move in straight lines at a fixed relative speed of 200 km/s.

Guided Inquiry

1 · What the observer sees

Set the lens mass to 1012 M⊙, the lens distance to 1 Gpc and the closest approach to 0.5 Einstein radii. Before pressing play, predict what the observer sees at the moment of closest approach.

2 · Magnification at closest approach

Keep the settings of question 1. Before pressing play, predict the total magnification at the moment of closest approach, when the source is 0.5 Einstein radii from the lens.

3 · A closer pass

Keep the lens mass at 1012 M⊙ and the lens distance at 1 Gpc, and set the closest approach to 0.1 Einstein radii. Before pressing play, predict the peak of the magnification curve.

4 · A star as the lens

Set the lens mass to 1 M⊙, the lens distance to 4 kpc and the closest approach to 0.5 Einstein radii. Before pressing play, predict what a telescope that separates angles of 0.1 arcsec records.

5 · Blue light and red light

Keep the settings of question 4. Before pressing play, predict how the curve measured in blue light compares with the curve measured in red light.

6 · How long the brightening lasts

Keep the settings of question 4. Before pressing play, predict the Einstein crossing time tE, which sets how long the brightening lasts, and compare it with the galaxy of question 1.

7 · What this shows

A point mass makes two images of a background source, on opposite sides of the lens, one outside and one inside the Einstein ring. Bending keeps the surface brightness, so the stretched images magnify the source by A = (u2 + 2)/(u√(u2 + 4)), which depends only on u and not on colour. The mass and the distances set only the scales, θE and tE. For a star in our Galaxy the images cannot be resolved: we see microlensing, a symmetric, achromatic brightening lasting about a month.

Lensing by a Point Mass

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A small, distant source drifts across the sky behind a point mass. The mass bends its light, and the sim shows what an observer sees and how bright the source becomes.

What you'll learn

  • How a point mass bends the light of a source behind it.
  • How the brightness of the source changes during the pass.
  • What sets the angular size and the duration of the event.
  • What a telescope records when the lens is a galaxy, and when it is a star.
The set-up on the sky, as the sim draws it, in units of the Einstein radius θE. The source moves along the dashed line, at closest approach u0 above the lens. Its distance from the lens is u.

What's on screen

  • Grey dot: the lens, a point mass.
  • Dashed circle: the Einstein ring, of radius θE.
  • Dotted circle: the true position of the source, moving along its dashed path. It is not what the observer sees.
  • Pale patches: the source as the observer sees it, lit by the sim at the source's own surface brightness.
  • Grey disc: the 0.1″ resolution of a large telescope, on the same scale.
  • Graph: the total magnification A against t/tE, in red light and in blue light.
See itLook at the opening arrangement. Watch for: the grey lens, the dashed ring around it, the dotted source on its dashed path, and the graph still empty at t/tE = −2.

03

Two images: one outside the ring, one inside

A point mass M bends a ray that passes at distance b by 4GM/c²b. Put the source at angle β from the lens, and let θ be the angle at which an image appears. The notes combine the two into the lens equation:

Equation (9.27). DL, DS and DLS are the distances to the lens, to the source, and from the lens to the source.

With β = 0 the image is a ring of radius θE, the Einstein ring. For β ≠ 0, multiplying by θ gives a quadratic, with two roots:

Equation (9.28). Both roots are images.

One image lies outside the ring on the same side of the lens as the source. The other lies inside the ring on the opposite side. In units of θE, with u = β/θE:

Equation (9.32), where y± = θ±/θE. The notes write η for the sim's u.
The source at u = 0.5 and its two images on one line through the lens.

At u = 0.5 the images sit at +1.28 and −0.78 θE, so the separation θ+ − θ− is θE√(u² + 4) = 2.06 θE. For the opening lens, 2.018″ per θE, that is 4.161″.

See itMove the source to its closest approach, at u = 0.5. Watch for: two pale patches on one line through the lens, one outside the dashed ring and one inside it, and the separation reading 4.161 arcsec.
04

Brightness: the images are stretched, so the source brightens

Bending does not change the surface brightness of a source (Section 3.3 of the notes). Each image has the source's surface brightness, so its brightness is proportional to its area. Round the lens, lengths are multiplied by y/u. Away from the lens they are multiplied by dy/du. The magnification of each image is A± = |(y±/u)(dy±/du)| (9.33), which comes to y±²/(u√(u² + 4)).

At u = 0.5 that gives A+ = 1.59 and A− = 0.59. The images carry opposite signs in y, and y+y− = −1, so the sum is:

Equation (9.34). The total magnification of a point source.
A against u. Far from the lens A tends to 1; for small u it follows 1/u, the dashed line.

At u = 0.5 the total is A = 2.18. At u = 1 it is 1.34. At u = 2 it is 1.06, close to 1, which is why the source looks undisturbed far from the lens. The sim writes A for a point source. Its drawn source has a small radius, 0.05 θE.

Key idea. A depends on u alone: the distance of the source from the lens, in Einstein radii.
See itPlay the pass up to closest approach. Watch for: A rising from about 1.06 while u falls, the source passing the lens, and the play stopping at the minimum of u.
05

A closer pass: a higher peak

The source moves in a straight line, so its distance from the lens changes with time as:

The notes' η(t), with t measured from closest approach. tE is the Einstein crossing time, taken up below.

Putting this into A(u) gives the light curves of the notes' Figure 103. They are symmetric about t = 0, and the peak is higher for smaller u0. The magnification A rises above 1.34, its value at u = 1, while |t| < √(1 − u0²) tE: for u0 = 0.5 that is 0.87 tE.

A(t) for four values of u0, from the sim's own point-lens function. The thicker curve is the opening u0 = 0.5.

At u0 = 0.1 the peak is A = 10.04, close to 1/u0 = 10. The images are then at +1.05 and −0.95 θE, both within about 5% of the ring. Each is stretched into a long arc along the ring, and the two arcs add up to the large A.

See itCompare u0 = 0.5 with u0 = 0.1 at closest approach. Watch for: the images stretching into long arcs close to the ring, and A going from 2.18 to 10.04.
06

The scales: mass and distance set only θE and tE

The mass and the distances enter through θE, which grows as M1/2 (9.27). A lens moving at v⊥ crosses the Einstein radius, of length DLθE in the plane of the lens, in the Einstein crossing time:

Equation (9.35). The sim fixes v⊥ = 200 km/s.

Both scales depend on M, but A(u) and the image positions in units of θE do not. A lens of 1012 M☉ at 1 Gpc and a lens of 1 M☉ at 4 kpc therefore draw the same A against t/tE for the same u0. Only the clock and the angles change:

Galaxy lensStar lens
M, DL1012 M☉, 1 Gpc1 M☉, 4 kpc
θE2.018″1.009 mas
tE4.78 × 107 yr35 days
Peak A at u0 = 0.52.182.18

The two values of θE differ by a factor of 2000, and the two values of tE by 5 × 108. Because tE ∝ M1/2, a hundred times less mass shortens the event by a factor of 10 at the same distance.

Key idea. The mass and the distances set the scales of the event, in angle and in time. The shape of the light curve is fixed by u0.
See itGo from the galaxy lens to the star lens at the same u0. Watch for: the readouts of θE and tE collapsing, while u and A at closest approach stay as they were.
07

Microlensing: when the images cannot be told apart

A telescope sees two images apart only if they are further apart than its resolution. For the star lens at u = 0.5 the separation is 2.08 mas, and the sim's 0.1″ disc is 99 θE across, so the whole pair fits inside it, as the figure shows; in the sim the disc covers the whole sky panel. The telescope records one spot, whose total brightness is A. Lensing without resolved images is called microlensing (Section 9.3).

On a log axis, the separation of the two images at u = 0.5 for the star lens and for the galaxy lens, against the 0.1″ resolution.

The spot brightens to about 2.2 times its usual value, then fades again over a time of order tE, which is 35 days here. Because the deflection 4GM/c²b does not depend on wavelength, the light curve is the same in blue and in red, and it is symmetric in time. The notes add that it is not repeated, which distinguishes it from a variable star.

The sim draws one function twice, blue dashes over a red line, so the match is built in. In the sky it is a measurable test.

Key idea. Without resolved images, the evidence is the shape of the light curve: symmetric, the same in every colour, and not repeated.
See itSwitch to the star lens and go to closest approach. Watch for: the grey disc covering the whole sky panel, A reading 2.18, and the blue dashes lying on the red line.
08

Where it matters: weighing lenses and searching the halo

A measured Einstein radius weighs the lens. Equation (9.29) of the notes gives the mass inside a cylinder of radius DLθE about the line of sight, whatever the matter is doing inside it. Behind rich clusters, background galaxies are stretched into arcs along the cluster's ring, of radius tens of arcseconds, and the masses found agree with the virial and X-ray masses to within a factor of order one.

The point-lens case is the exact one for a star or other compact object. If the dark matter of the Milky Way's halo were compact bodies, one would see microlensing events as they cross lines of sight to the Magellanic Clouds. A lens of half a solar mass in the halo has a crossing time of order a month. The chance that a given star is being lensed at any moment is below 10−6, so the MACHO, EROS and OGLE surveys followed tens of millions of stars for years. They found far fewer events than such a halo would give, and concluded that compact objects between roughly 10−7 and 10 M☉ make up at most a small fraction of it.

The sim uses a single point lens. A real galaxy or cluster is extended, so its images and magnifications differ from these.

09

Summary

In one line. A point mass bends the light of a source behind it, and what an observer sees depends on the closest approach, the mass and the distances.

Common mix-ups

  • "A heavier lens makes a taller peak." A 1012 M☉ lens and a 1 M☉ lens both peak at A = 2.18 for u0 = 0.5. The mass stretches the axes only.
  • "The blue light must peak differently from the red." The deflection does not depend on wavelength, so the two curves coincide.
  • "There is only one image." There are two, one outside the ring and one inside it. At u = 0.5 they carry A+ = 1.59 and A− = 0.59.
  • "A galaxy lens brightens a source while you watch." Its tE is 4.78 × 107 yr. Only stellar lenses vary on a human timescale.

Things to try on your own

  • Set u0 = 1.00. The peak should read A = 1.34.
  • Set M = 0.1 M☉ and DL = 1 kpc. tE should read about 5.5 days, and θE about 0.64 mas.
